items.title: Letters to Oscar Wilde from correspondents A-H and unidentified correspondents

matches.what: Hotel d'Alsace bill, J. Dupoirier, 13 Rue des Beaux-Arts - the hotel where Wilde died. Two images, the second a photographic negative of the first

To Wilde from an artist at Studio, 53 Mortimer Street, Cavendish Square, 'Monday 28th April' - fixing a sitting for Thursday at five, postscript asking him to bring a couple of his latest photographs. Signature not yet read

Lawrence Alma-Tadema to Wilde, 18 July 1881, Townshend House, Regents Park - supplying the Greek forms of the names of Sappho's circle: Anactoria of Miletus, Gongyla of Colophon, Gyrinna, Atthis, Erinna of Telos, Mnasidica, with the Aeolic spellings and the genitives of Apollo and Artemis taken off a Greek pot
To Wilde from the Athenaeum Club, 'Sunday' - the writer is off to Spain and asks Wilde to call on Count Bozenta Chlapowski, husband of the actress Helena Modjeska
Hamilton Aide to Wilde - commending Modjeska before her London appearance, 'a very gifted and sympathetic woman', with the Chlapowskis' address at 6 Half Moon Street
George Alexander to Wilde, 21 July 1892, St James's Theatre - placing money to Wilde's credit at the bank during the run of Lady Windermere's Fan, and on the autumn prospects

William Archer to Wilde, 29 May 1894, 40 Queen Square - proposing a weekly theatrical causerie for the Pall Mall Budget, and asking whether Lewis Waller is to produce a play of Wilde's at the Haymarket during Tree's absence, and whether he may announce the title

Matthew Arnold to Wilde, 9 July [1881], Pains Hill Cottage, Cobham - acknowledging the presentation copy of Poems: 'I perceive in them the true feeling for rhythm, which is at the bottom of all success in poetry'. He goes on that one 'must shake off London life before one can do one's best work', and closes 'from my fellow writers, both in poetry and prose, I have met with kindness and recognition such as might satisfy any man'

To Wilde from 18 Berkeley Square, annotated 'November 9' - thanking him for a volume and weighing a request for an article: 'The subject is a very delicate one, and there is always the fear of treading on toes! How long should the article be?' Kind regards to Mrs Wilde. Signature not yet read

Frank R. Benson to Wilde, Newport, Wednesday - thanking him for a photograph and a kind letter which reached the actor 'as I was going on for Hamlet' before an apple-eating, nut-cracking house, and on what he learned from Hermann Vezin about playing Othello: 'I hope to be an actor some day, there is so much crudeness and roughness in my efforts at present'

William Blackwood to Wilde, 29 May 1889, 45 George Street, Edinburgh - on placing 'The Portrait of Mr W. H.' in Blackwood's Magazine, the July number being full, and on copyright: he proposes using the story in the new series of 'Tales from Blackwood' as an equivalent for the copyright, 'which would thus remain your property'

Jacques-Emile Blanche to Wilde, Dimanche, Paris Auteuil - sending a ticket for the vernissage to Wilde's hotel, or else to meet him at half past one before the door of the palais; and asking for news of the Grosvenor

Wilfrid Scawen Blunt to Wilde, 13 July, 10 James Street, Buckingham Gate - inviting him to Crabbet Park, Three Bridges, for Saturday 28 July, 'to see my horses and meet some of my friends'; the four o'clock train from Victoria will be met

Arthur Bourchier to Wilde, Wednesday, Christ Church, Oxford - 'Is it true that there is a chance of your paying a visit to this benighted place on Saturday next? If so, may I trust that you will come as my guest?'

Paul Bourget to Wilde, in French, from 2 Walton Place, S.W. - back from the Isle of Wight and Manderston and leaving for Oxford at the end of the week, proposing an evening together; compliments to Mrs Wilde

Oscar Browning to Wilde, 29 May 1879, King's College, Cambridge - chasing two small commissions he had asked Wilde to do in London, which 'can only be executed (1) by somebody in London (2) by a man of taste', and asking him to visit

Robert Buchanan to Wilde, 5 August 1891, 25 Maresfield Gardens - thanking him for The Picture of Dorian Gray and arguing with it at length. 'You seem to me like a lightly-clad urchin throwing pebbles into the sea'; 'Dorian Gray is very very clever. It is more - it is masterly and stimulating, and had (though you may not know it) the anxiety of a human soul in it'; 'You care far less about Art, or any other word-spells with a capital, than you are willing to admit, and thereby lies your salvation'; and 'One catches you constantly in puris naturalibus, and then the Man is worth observing'

Edward Burne-Jones to Constance Wilde - the engagement is too sudden to go tomorrow, but he will write to the housekeeper at Mrs Graham's, 35 Grosvenor Place, the family being abroad, and she will show her everything; he mentions calling with Bastien-Lepage
Jean-Charles Cazin to Wilde, in French, Dimanche - his card was already addressed and on the table when Wilde's request arrived

C. Haddon Chambers to Wilde, Friday - sending 'The Collaborators' and hoping Wilde will get Hawtrey to read it, with Hawtrey and Penley in mind for the parts. Postscript: 'I am going to do the little gold nugget story almost at once. The motif charms me. But ought I to use your plot as my own?'
Lady Churchill to Wilde, 6 July 1888, Osborne - she has received the copy of The Woman's World and shown it to the Queen, who 'likes the Poem very much, composed by Lady Wilde, and has read it'

Stephen Coleridge to Wilde, 19 March 1890, 7 Egerton Mansions - sending 'The Sanctity of Confession' and claiming for it 'two qualities that should recommend it to you: one its brevity, and the other its English. There are but two living writers in this England who observe a true reverence for their immortal language. I am one; you are the other.' He hopes the next volume of stories will not be long delayed
Constant Coquelin to Wilde, in French - asking him to come tomorrow, Saturday, at half past nine: 'Nous causerons de ce qui vous interesse'
To Wilde from the Garrick Club, 19 February - thanking him for the present of Lady Windermere's Fan, 'a worthy frame for so clever a piece'. Signature not yet read

Walter Crane to Wilde, 15 June 1888, Beaumont Lodge, Shepherd's Bush - on The Happy Prince and Other Tales, which he illustrated: the children 'have been treated well and have sumptuous margins', and Jacomb Hood's headings and ornaments and cover are praised

F. Marion Crawford to Wilde, Monday morning, 241 Beacon Street, Boston - arranging for Mr Munzig to call at half past three and drive him out to the Institution where Mrs Anagnos lives. 1882 American tour
To Wilde, 7 March - on the writer's Shelley in the February number of the North American Review, lines on Browning and Dante, and the forthcoming book. Correspondent not yet identified

Aubrey de Vere to Wilde, 16 June [1878] - congratulating him on winning the Newdigate Prize, 'considered one of the chief academical distinctions', glad it 'should have fallen to an Irishman and to you', and dwelling on the gratification it will be to his mother

Emilia Dilke to Wilde, 12 November 1884, 1 Hyde Park Gate - asking him to call on Lady Harberton at 119 Cromwell Road to discuss 'the all-important question of dress'; Lady Harberton 'admires much of your last Pall Mall article but has I believe some suggestions to make'

Edgar Fawcett to Wilde, 10 November [1882], Union Club, Fifth Avenue and 21st Street, New York - reminding him of dinner at seven: 'Your entertainers are to be: Martin Van Buren, Frankie Riggs and myself. We shall expect you to be in your very most charming and brilliant mood'

W. E. Gladstone to Wilde, 1 November 1888, Hawarden Castle - declining to sign the memorial got up on behalf of Lady Wilde. 'From the printed Memorial, and even apart from the painful circumstances which you mention, I should as a reader suppose Lady Wilde's claim to be a very good one: but I am sorry to say I am not in a condition to sign the paper', having made a rigid rule against memorials of that nature and preferring to write separately where he has personal knowledge

Edmund Gosse to Wilde, 15 December 1893, 29 Delamere Terrace - on the printed Lady Windermere's Fan, 'the brilliant merit of which is only enhanced by the absence of stage disturbance... We might still have a drama, if they would only close the play-houses'

John Hare to Wilde, 3 Park Crescent - refusing to be hurried over a play. He will answer definitely on Thursday, will not surrender 'a comedy that suits me so well in many respects, simply because another manager importunes you for a ready-made play', and will either return the manuscript or settle the production at the Garrick

Frank Harris to Wilde, 15 February 1890, The Fortnightly Review office - the earliest Harris letter here, and a commission: 'Our lunch today has made me wish that you would write an Article for the March Fortnightly. Can you do this within 8 days? An Article on Literature or any Social Subject as paradoxical as you please'
William Heinemann to Wilde, 26 September 1893, 21 Bedford Street - inviting him to lunch on Friday to meet Zola

Princess Christian to Wilde, 28 March, Cumberland Lodge, Windsor Park - thanking him for his note and cheque, glad her little article met with his approval, and asking that six copies of the April number of The Woman's World be sent to her
To Wilde, a long letter mentioning 'Poems of Sorrow' and the writer's brother. Correspondent not yet identified

John Hollingshead to Wilde, 14 March 1883, Gaiety Theatre, Strand - on stage management, which he claims to have been first to discuss in the Fortnightly: 'You speak on artistic subjects with more authority than I do. It is now stage-carpenter v. scene-painter. It will soon be stage-bricklayer v. stage-carpenter'. The verso carries pencil sums

Lord Houghton (Richard Monckton Milnes) to Wilde, 20 May [1877], 24 Arlington Street - on Wilde's sonnet at Keats's grave: 'Thanks for your sonnet which is tender and graceful but not true. My life of Keats shows that he was anything but unhappy and he was recognized with unusual rapidity. The medallion is very like him and having been put up by enthusiastic friends it would not do to try to displace it.' Postscript: 'Give my best regards to Mr Mahaffy and tell him to let me know when he comes to London'
A pen-and-ink sketch on grey paper, unsigned - not a letter
Modern typed transcript of the Houghton letter at images 63-64, with manuscript corrections - curatorial, not an original

items.title: Letters to Oscar Wilde from correspondents I-R

matches.what: To Wilde from the Royal Lyceum Theatre, Strand, 14 November - short note of thanks. Signature not yet read; the Lyceum is Irving's house and Bram Stoker was his manager
Madge Kendal to Wilde, 145 Harley Street - 'the law of the Medes and Persians'

Louise Jopling to Wilde, Thursday, 28 Beaufort Street, Chelsea Embankment - she is going to Oxford on the 29th to hear Ruskin lecture and asks Wilde for a letter of introduction; she was sorry 'you two could not come to me on my birthday'

John Lane to Wilde, 8 June 1893, Elkin Mathews and John Lane, The Bodley Head - sending a specimen page of Lady Windermere's Fan, wanting Act I, and reporting 'I have this day seen Beardsley and arranged for a title and a cover for 50 guineas!'
To Wilde from 'Woodfield' - thanking him for Ravenna, which the writer had already read and 'called it mine', Mr Lacy having sent it; hoping to see him on the 28th. Correspondent not yet identified

To Wilde from a woman poet - on his 'Time' and her own verses: 'I like to think that we mutually admire each other... you, who are young, are above all, a man... For a poor woman like me, all I can do is to write poorly'. Correspondent not yet identified

Lillie Langtry to Wilde, Monday, from the telegraph station at Shipley, Derby - 'I am so disgusted with myself for forgetting entirely till this moment all about the brougham. I cannot forgive myself so must implore you to forgive me instead. How is Ellen Terry?'
Richard Le Gallienne to Wilde, 14 January, Mulberry Cottage, Brentford - sending a copy of his verses
Charles Godfrey Leland to Wilde, 21 October 1879, 22 Park Square East - on enlisting Professor Palmer and Walter Besant, on everybody being out of town, and with regards to Lady Wilde
To Wilde, Wednesday - short note. Signature not yet read

George Lewis to Wilde, 25 August 1882, Lewis & Lewis, Ely Place, addressed care of D'Oyly Carte at 1267 Broadway, New York - on the American tour. He has telegraphed Colt not to discharge Morse as manager, and urges Wilde to avoid disputes: 'any sort of breach or show of anger on either side might be injurious to the success of the undertaking'. He is glad of the reception, tells him to look for paid work as a newspaper correspondent, and adds 'take care and save some money'. London papers, he says, print telegrams about Wilde constantly, 'and your doings are almost as much publicly read here as in America'

George Lewis to Wilde, 7 July 1894, Lewis & Lewis, Ely Place - THE WITHDRAWAL. 'The information that you have received that I am acting for Lord Queensberry is perfectly correct, and under these circumstances you will at once see that it is impossible for me to offer any opinion about any proceedings you intend to take against him. Although I cannot act against him, I should not act against you.' Read on the sheet by Lovelle 2026-08-10; I had transcribed 'shall not', which would be a promise where 'should not' is a statement of what would be proper - the more lawyerly of the two, and the one on the page. Addressed to 16 Tite Street. Nine months before the libel action
To Wilde, Sunday, 14 Carlton House Terrace - apologising for missing an engagement on the Thursday, going away for a week, and proposing 'we must do another play'. Signature not yet read

Pierre Louys to Wilde, 28 May 1892, on pink paper - thanking him for his photograph and asking for a word before he leaves for London. The printer is waiting for Wilde's cheque to begin setting Salome: he asks 202 + 50 plus a supplement for the de luxe papers, about 285 in all. Jacques-Emile Blanche has begun his portrait and Regnier's, and 'nous attendons Andre Gide qui est toujours en Allemagne et me parle souvent de vous dans ses lettres'. He wants to meet Wilde at Lady Windermere's Fan rather than at his house, about 10 June
To Wilde from a correspondent writing under a coronet, Saturday - thanking him for a gift of his work and looking forward to seeing him during a visit to Paris. Correspondent not yet identified

Maurice Macmillan to Wilde, 16 June 1890, Macmillan & Co, Bedford Street - refusing The Picture of Dorian Gray. 'It is a weird tale and some of the conversation is most brilliant. I am afraid however that it would not do for us to publish. We have done very little in the way of such strong situations, and I confess there is something in the power which Dorian Gray gets over the young natural scientist, and one or two other things, which is rather repelling. I dare say you do not mean it to be. I am sure it is not for us, and I do not like to keep it any longer'

Stephane Mallarme to Wilde, in French - on Salome. He begs to be excused for not thanking him sooner 'de votre mysterieuse, etrange et admirable Salome', and says he says merci today for the third time
J. P. Mahaffy to Wilde, Tuesday, Athenaeum Club - 'Carissimo amico', on calling at Wilde's house late at night and finding everyone out

Stephane Mallarme to Wilde, Paris, Mars - a second and fuller letter on Salome. 'J'admire que tout etant exprime par des perpetuels traits eblouissants, en votre Salome, il se degage, aussi, a chaque page, de l'indicible et le Songe. Ainsi les gemmes innombrables et exactes ne peuvent servir que d'accompagnement sur sa robe au geste surnaturel de cette jeune princesse, que definitivement vous evoquates'

Richard Mansfield to Wilde, 15 August 1888, 183 Piccadilly - on Wilde's kind letter and words of approval, and on his own exhaustion: 'This is the result of the few weeks of holiday, the first in four years of incessant toil'
Jeanette L. Martin to Wilde, February 4, 31 Onslow Square - on meeting his mother, and on Lady Wilde

Elkin Mathews to Wilde, 24 October 1891, The Bodley Head, Vigo Street - the terms for issuing Poems: 230 copies with his imprint, a cover design at 5 pounds 5 shillings, block, binding and advertising to be first charges on receipts, advertising not to exceed 5 pounds 5 shillings, his commission 20 per cent on the net published price, the book to be brought out as a net one, balance remitted quarterly, the first six months after publication

Elkin Mathews to Wilde, 25 February 1892, The Bodley Head - on the binding of Poems. Ricketts will have received specimen cases; he saw one 'done up in the darker cloth, and the gold design looked splendid', and urges Wilde to choose that cloth rather than a pale one, which gets dirty. The binders report the 230 copies will fall short by ten through spoiled sheets

Wilfrid Meynell to Wilde, Saturday, The Weekly Register, 43 Essex Street, Strand - 'I wish you would pronounce ex cathedra (on a postcard)' on a question, and referring to an article on Newman in the week's issue
Mortimer Menpes to Wilde, Osborn Lodge, Fulham - on an element of satire in a portrait, and on the history of caricature; he has tried some, including Swinburne and Burne-Jones
Alfred Milner to Wilde, 11 November 1878, 54 Claverton Street - sorry he cannot come on Wednesday and meet Barmann; hoping Wilde means to stay in Oxford till the end of term

Helena Modjeska to Wilde, Tuesday, under a coronet monogram - sorry she was not able to come, Bosenta being unwell and unable to accompany her; 'it is true that an old woman like me ought not to be afraid to go about alone, but it is always better to avoid danger'. She mentions Cassandra

William Morris to Wilde, 5 January 1893, Kelmscott House, Upper Mall, Hammersmith - 'I am told that Lady Wilde, your mother, was the translatress of a book which was much read and liked by our clique some twenty five or thirty years ago', now long out of print. He wants to print a small edition, say 350, at the Kelmscott Press, and asks Wilde to lay the request before her and ask what she would think a proper honorarium. The book is Sidonia the Sorceress. 'I propose printing the book just as it stands, errors of the press excepted, as I hate alterations years after the date of the first issue'

To Wilde from the editor of The Artist, 24 Redcliffe Road, South Kensington - 'You may perhaps have heard that I have undertaken the Editorship of The Artist. I write to ask a favour of you: may I once more interview you in quite a private way to learn your opinion on an ideal mode of life?'
To Wilde from The Artist - continuation of image 48, recalling 'a very pleasant interview some two years ago' and hoping 'we are shortly to be charmed by another of your plays'
Lady Dorothy Nevill to Wilde, 45 Charles Street, Berkeley Square - 'I am here no one else. When shall I see you? Will you come on Tuesday morning at 12?'

Lady Dorothy Nevill to Wilde, 45 Charles Street - 'I cannot get access from myself to think of you in a dull existence, but never mind, I shall be mistress of the situation whenever you will bring your wife to see me - but do not come till after next week as I am going out of London'; thanks for a newspaper from Hotel Waynecute and messages to Lady Hoppy
Lady Dorothy Nevill to Wilde, 17th - 'Will you and Mrs Wilde come and see me about 4 on Thursday next. I have been away and at this dreadful season one has no time for anything'
Curatorial slip: 'Lady Dorothy Nevill to O.W.' - identifying the preceding letters, not itself a document

To Wilde from Bradmore Road, Oxford, July 14 - thanking him for the magazine and his letter: 'Your excellent article on the Grosvenor Gallery I read with very great pleasure; it makes me much wish to make your acquaintance, and I hope you will give me an early call on your return to Oxford'. Signature on the following image

Walter Pater to Wilde - 'I should much like to talk over some of the points with you. Though on the whole I think your criticism very just, and it is exclusively very pleasantly expressed. It shows that you possess some beautiful, and I am sure appreciative and exquisitely cultivated taste, and a considerable knowledge also of many beautiful things. I hope you will write a great deal in time to come'. This is the signature leaf of the Bradmore Road letter at image 56

Walter Palmer to Wilde, 15 February 1895, 49 Upper Brook Street - 'My warmest congratulations on your excellent play, the two latter acts of which I had the delight of seeing on Thursday', having got in after some contest with the manager by using Wilde's name. The Importance of Being Earnest opened on 14 February 1895

Sir Noel Paton to Wilde, Wednesday night, 33 George Square - 'I am always in a sad muddle of occupation; but not, I regret to say, always in the service of the queen Titania of Art!'; arranging a meeting round committee meetings, with mention of Mrs Wilde
To Wilde, 22 September - 'We do not publish translations in this country'. Signature not yet read
Christine Nilsson Rouzaud to Wilde, in French, Dimanche - thanking him for the volume of poems he sent so graciously, which she will read with great pleasure when she has a moment to herself

Henri de Regnier to Wilde, in French, Dimanche, 6 rue Boccador - proposing to call for Wilde on Saturday at four and take him together to Heredia's, as they had discussed; if the hour or the place does not suit, Wilde is to name his own

T. Wemyss Reid to Wilde, 24 March 1890, The Speaker, 115 Fleet Street - he will use 'the admirable wisdom of your Sage', but must ask Wilde to back it with his name, 'otherwise all the nonconformists will rise against you, and my life will not be safe in the hands of any shopkeeper who reads the Speaker'

Rennell Rodd to Wilde, 24 Beaufort Gardens - on Wilde's American tour. He encloses a cutting from Truth and observes 'you are indeed lucky to have both Yates and L on your side. Well, you seem to be having amazing fun over there. We all feel a little jealous.' He reports the story of Wilde declining to eat on hearing the ladies were upstairs, has seen Lady Wilde - 'we jubilated over you' - and adds 'I wish I could have been with you when you went to see Walt Whitman'

W. B. Richmond to Wilde, on mourning paper - a long letter of advice on the book Wilde has sent. 'Don't be the Hero of an hour! Don't mind what critics say if you are quite certain all your thoughts have been sincere... there comes a time when the strength is proved and endurance is certain, when the fetters have to be broken... Don't be led astray by the clever word painting of modern poetry, however great the charm of it may be... don't live on the success of early efforts, look forward to the horizon of your own possibilities, and grasp your own individuality with an iron and even ugly hand'

Norman Forbes-Robertson to Wilde, 20 March 1899, 24 Charlotte Street, Bedford Square - sorry he could not call, 'especially as I should have had you all to myself', having had an engagement to dine with a friend; he will call another day, wanting to hear about Wilde's poem

William Michael Rossetti to Wilde, 3 August 1877, Marine House, Gorleston, Great Yarmouth - thanking him for his letter and the magazine containing 'your interesting little article about the grave of Keats'. On a Keats memorial: 'No doubt English people ought to erect a statue to Keats, and I should be glad to lend my modest cooperation to any such project. I don't however see any particular opening for it at present. I will confess also that I felt more especially interested in Shelley than in Keats: I did some while ago, when the Byron statue was first projected, put into print a strong suggestion that advantage might be taken of the movement so as to combine a Shelley with a Byron memorial, but it led to nothing. All three must get their statues some day, and doubtless will'

John Ruskin to Wilde - 'I am greatly vexed to see from your note that you have never got mine written on Saturday to explain my seeming neglect. I hope it may still reach you. Thursday will do delightfully for me. Ever gratefully yours'

items.title: Letters to Oscar Wilde from correspondents S-Z

matches.what: To Wilde from a painter, Tuesday - inviting him to the studio tomorrow afternoon or Thursday morning, 'you will find me still working at my portrait of Mrs ---'; the picture goes to the Salon on Thursday if it is finished and good, and if the servants say he is out Wilde must knock at the door himself, 'toc toc'. Another work, 'La Phryne', is mentioned. Correspondent not yet identified
Frederick Sandys to Wilde - two fragments, one a clipped signature strip, 'Yours faithfully Frederick Sandys'

A. H. Sayce to Wilde, 17 November 1878, Queen's College, Oxford - 'Don't engage yourself for next Sunday, as Macmillan is coming to me on Saturday; so I want you to dine with us in Hall at 6. If you don't take your degree next Thursday come without cap and gown'

Olive Schreiner to Wilde, Rosemarto, Harpenden - 'Please be sure to send me the proofs. I wrote the thing in a letter to a friend two years ago; they copied it out and sent me the MS, but I've never re-read it, and it may need alteration.' She has been living 'here in a little cottage quite by myself for three months' and goes abroad again in a couple of weeks

Marcel Schwob to Wilde, Lundi matin, 2 rue de l'Universite, Paris - glad of the date Wilde has fixed, which lets him hope they will meet again before he leaves. 'Je crois qu'Aristide Bruant vous interesse. Je le connais beaucoup, et nous pourrions nous arranger avec A. Gide pour aller dejeuner chez lui, tout en haut de la Butte Montmartre.' Meanwhile he expects Wilde at his rooms - 'they are frightfully small and the ceiling very low' - from noon, to lunch at Laperouse or the restaurant Mignon

To Wilde, 13 March, signed Speed - recalling his visit to 'the dingy old house' and the pleasure he gave 'by the tender interest with which you touched the Fuseli manuscripts and the Milton', only the third time the writer had shown them since they came into their possession. Correspondent not securely identified; the surname is legible, the forenames are not

Dorothy Tennant to Wilde, 9 April - thanking him for a charming 'real child's story' and for the poems of his friend Mr Todd, whom she has since met in London: 'I know of your friendship as he speaks of you with affectionate admiration'

TYPED TRANSCRIPTS, not originals - a curatorial set on punched ruled paper transcribing letters to Wilde, each marked A.L.S.: Stephen Coleridge (19 March 1890), Frank Harris (Fortnightly Review office, February 1890), T. Wemyss Reid (The Speaker, 24 January 1890), James Payn, W. T. Stead (Review of Reviews, 4 August 1893), Charles Lever, W. E. Gladstone (Hawarden, 1 November 1888) and Edmund Yates (1 York Street, Covent Garden, 20 May 1879). Several of the originals are elsewhere in this collection; no emphasis claim can rest on a transcript
Cover of a letter of introduction carried by Wilde on the American tour: 'Favoured by Oscar Wilde', to E. C. Stedman Esq, 5 Pine Street, New York

Newspaper clipping describing a New York reception for Louisa M. Alcott at which Wilde was present, with a full account of his dress - 'black trousers with knee buckles, black silk stockings, and low, tied shoes; also a black frock-coat over a low-cut white waistcoat. A large, lone diamond stud shone in his shirt bosom' - and a long guest list including Robert Roosevelt, W. F. Morse and William Sartain. The verso carries California stock prices for 7 January 1882, which dates the cutting

W. T. Stead to Wilde, 4 August 1893, The Review of Reviews - TYPEWRITTEN. Introducing Mrs Gattie, whose reception by Wilde may prevent 'a good deal of mischief that might possibly terminate in a law-suit', since 'I consider it to be the duty of every civilized man to prevent any of this world's wealth going to the legal fraternity'. He closes: 'It is ages and ages since I saw you, but, of course, like everyone else, from time to time, you compel the attention even of those who occupy the court of the gentiles'

John Addington Symonds to Wilde, 13 July 1890, Davos - on The Portrait of Mr W. H. He apologises for a note in his own book which seemed to slight Wilde's essay on the Sonnets, says it 'ought to have been deleted in the proofs' and is 'obviously a mere obiter dictum', offers 'some public reparation', and asks Wilde to send him a copy of the essay: 'The hypothesis is ingenious, and I should much like to examine it again at leisure.' He describes his own poem on a boy-actor in the London theatre of Shakespeare's day, imagining an Italian visitor 'being greatly smitten on his arrival with the person who played Bellario in Fletcher's Philaster'. The last leaf is Davos in deep snow

Ellen Terry to Wilde, 18 February 1881 - 'I've a box for The Cup next Thursday. My friend Miss Codrington is going, my friend Justin is going. If you're not going anywhere else, will you fetch me at 10 o'clock at the Lyceum and we'll go too? I'll order my rattle-trap to be at the stage door and compel you to get inside and wait instead of shivering at the horrible stage door. Have you recovered the spite of the distracted Globe?'

Herbert Beerbohm Tree to Wilde, 12 August, Queen Down Warren, near Sittingbourne - returning a play he read 'with great interest and which I considered dramatic and stirring'. He thinks it would gain by cutting, 'the dialogue is here and there somewhat redundant and the heroine's passions struck me as too fluctuating for theatrical purposes', but finds 'great force and picturesqueness in it all'. He asks about a new play, sends his wife's regards, and adds a postscript
Maud Beerbohm Tree to Wilde, 77 Sloane Street - thanking him 'for the sweet flattery of your pretty inscription'
Maud Beerbohm Tree to Wilde, continued - on A Woman of No Importance 'in its production as a stage-play' and 'in its production as a book alas!'
Henry Vezin to Wilde, 25 March, Bernard Vezin, 10 Lancaster Place, Strand - 'You left your cheque book and legal document here. I would enclose them but don't know your number under it'
Pierre Loti to Wilde, on monogrammed paper - 'Merci, monsieur, de m'avoir fait connaitre votre Salome. C'est beau et sombre comme un chapitre de l'Apocalypse. Je l'admire profondement'

Lewis Waller to Wilde, 18 August 1894, The Walsingham House, Piccadilly - 'Tree consents to Mrs Pat Campbell. Now we want her consent. Please see her as soon as possible and read play to her, or if not convenient I will'

Genevieve Ward to Wilde, 25 February 1880, Corda Lodge, 10 Cavendish Road, St John's Wood - 'The umbrellas got terribly mixed last Monday at my house. If you are not rightly umbrellaged, will you kindly drop me a line describing yours and I will bring it down to the Prince of Wales's, where together we will give it back to you and receive the wandering wild one'

To Wilde, June, The Priory, Aubrey Hill(?) - the writer was inspired by 'the charming little damsels' seen while driving home yesterday afternoon and encloses verses, asking Wilde to send Mrs Wilde's autograph book. Signature not yet read

Theodore Watts(-Dunton) to Wilde - on Wilde's prose tales: 'Your fairy stories charmed me; but why not write them in verse? Verse only lives and dies on woman's pain to any praise to have a strong motif'

Constance, Duchess of Westminster, to Wilde, 4 January, Eaton, Chester - enclosing a cheque for 10 pounds from her husband, 'indeed for a most deserving sad case'. She excuses the scrawl by 'the agonies of a rehearsal for a Play, for this very evening, and that Ronald is screaming for me'; and asks whether 'Mrs Langtry's portrait would not be cast aside'

To Wilde, Sunday night - 'Dear Oscar, you have simply to get on your disguise again and come off with me tomorrow to Surrey. I shall be down at the studio tomorrow and shall send for you at about 12; we can make our final arrangements and probably leave by the 5 o'clock train'. Signature not read; a seal is impressed at the foot

To Wilde - 'Carissimo! I have unwittingly broken the seal of the enclosed. Milles pardons. I have read nothing but the first word, Election, and know not who it is from. So you must tell me when we meet'

Edmund Yates to Wilde, Tuesday 20 May 1879, 1 York Street, Covent Garden - 'I am very sorry that I shall not be able to use your poem in the June number and I hope you will allow it to stand over until July. I have an eight page poem of Mrs Singleton's on a subject of the day, Killed at Isandula, and a two page poem of Mr Sandmonde's which has been in my hands for three months, and this is all the verse I can afford space for in one number'. He adds that Wilde shall have proof of the Chevy Chase as soon as possible

items.title: Third-Party correspondence from individuals A-H and unidentified correspondents

matches.what: Not correspondence. Printed leaves extracted from Bernard Shaw, Plays and Players: Essays on the Theatre (Oxford, The World's Classics, 1952), carrying his Saturday Review notice 'Two New Plays' of 12 January 1895 on Henry James's Guy Domville and Wilde's An Ideal Husband, and 'Poor Shakespear!' of 2 February 1895. The title page carries a manuscript covering note, not Wilde's: 'Dear Ed: the 2nd play reviewed in this series is Wilde's Ideal Husband. Shaw understood its genius and glowed with praise - whereas he condemned The Importance of Being Earnest.' Passages on Wilde are marked in the margin. Useful as reception evidence, but a printed book, and the sentences are Shaw's published text rather than anything unpublished

Fr Edmund Burke C.P., Rector, St Paul's Retreat, Mount Argus, Dublin, to H. Montgomery Hyde MP, 4 February and 19 March 1955 - 20th-century scholarly correspondence about FATHER CUTHBERT DUNNE, the Passionist who received Wilde into the Catholic Church as he was dying. Fr Dunne 'was always very reticent about details, but he had carefully preserved all the material relating to the fact. This includes letters from Robert Ross relative to the funeral and burial arrangements, clippings from contemporary Paris and London papers, letters from David Hunter-Blair, and a letter which Mr Vyvyan Holland wrote as a boy from Stonyhurst.' At Burke's suggestion Fr Dunne wrote a memoir of the scene; he died in Dublin in 1950, aged 31 when he was called to Wilde

H. Montgomery Hyde to Fr Edmund Burke, 24 February 1955 - he has handed the letter to Vyvyan Holland, was in Paris for the fiftieth anniversary of Wilde's death and spoke at Pere Lachaise, and the evening before took Mrs Holland and Mrs Ross, a niece of Robert Ross, to the Hotel d'Alsace. He notes that he has in his own Wilde collection 'the last bill rendered by the hotel to Wilde as he was dying, and which was paid by Ross'

TYPESCRIPT, 'Extracts from Memoir of Father Cuthbert Dunne, C.P.' - the priest's own account of Wilde's deathbed. Ross, summoned by telegram from the South of France, came 'in great haste to avenue Roche, looking for a priest to minister to the dying man. I was the one he found.' Wilde was 'half-conscious, trying indeed to speak, yet not able to utter an articulate word'. Dunne administered Baptism and the other Sacraments, 'having ascertained the man's long-cherished desire to become a Catholic'. Wilde 'made a hard fight for life which lasted nearly three days'. Requiem Mass praesente cadavere at St Germain des Pres, burial at Bagneux, 'this however was to be only a temporary resting-place, for some years later the remains were transferred to the cemetery of Pere Lachaise'

Jane Cunningham Croly ('Jennie June') to a correspondent, 162 East 38th Street, 30 January - a long letter on journalism and literary society, and on the reception she gave for Miss Alcott at which Wilde appeared. 'I do not seek celebrities, however. I never invite anyone to come to our house who does not way or other come to me first.' She denies having originated a paragraph about 'the character of Oscar Wilde's entertainments' - 'I did not consider myself one of them, and it was afterward that I heard it attributed to you'. This is the other side of the Alcott reception clipping in item 2898

Maurice Cranston to H. Montgomery Hyde, 5 August 1954, Travellers' Club - asking when the true date of Wilde's birth was established: 'Until a few years ago it was always given as 1856 (the date Wilde himself gave), but somebody must have found out the true date, and I should like to know who'

H. Montgomery Hyde to Maurice Cranston, 11 October 1954 - 'There is no doubt that Wilde was born on October 16th, 1854 as his Birth Certificate clearly shows.' He mentions the unveiling of the plaque on Wilde's house in Tite Street by Compton Mackenzie

Printed invitation card: 'Mr Robert S. Davis requests the pleasure of your Company on Monday evening, January 16th 1882, from eight until ten o'clock, to meet Mr Oscar Wilde. 1804 Spruce Street. An early answer requested.' Philadelphia, on the American tour; annotated 'declined'

LORD ALFRED DOUGLAS to Franklin P. Rolfe, University of California, 30 December 1940, 1 St Ann's Court, Hove - refusing permission to publish Wilde's letters to Robert Ross that refer to him. 'I cannot see my way to giving my consent to the publication of references to me in Oscar Wilde's letters to Robert Ross which you describe as obviously and unquestionably libellous.' He calls Ross's character 'exposed by me in the Central Criminal Court at the Old Bailey before a Judge and Jury in 1914 when I established that he was, among other things, a blackmailer', cites his own Oscar Wilde: A Summing Up (Duckworth, 1940) describing Ross as 'the villain of the piece', and complains of 'a continual barrage of venomous abuse and insult from Wilde's biographers, chiefly in the U.S.A.' He adds that his nephew Lord Queensberry would not consent either, objecting to the attacks on his brother, Lord Queensberry's father. Forty-five years after the trials, still refusing

LORD ALFRED DOUGLAS to the editor of the Review of Reviews, 28 June 1895, Hotel de la Poste, Rouen - six sides, written seven weeks after Wilde was sentenced and while he was in prison. Douglas is 25. Held as photographic negatives, white-on-black AND laterally reversed; they must be inverted and mirrored to be read. He answers W. T. Stead's article on the case. He grants Stead is 'a man with a conscience' but attacks him for upholding 'the horrible and barbarous law which condemns a man who is guilty of these so-called offences to a sentence which you calmly describe as probably capital'. His central argument is the one still made: 'Everything that diverges from the normal may to a certain extent be called unnatural, genius and beauty among them.' And then the comparison that gives the letter its force - such laws 'do not exist in France, and there these offences are ignored by the law just as fornication is ignored in England, and yet you will hardly venture to say that this taint or suspicion exists in connection with friendships between people of the same sex in France'. He then argues from women: 'in England there are no laws against Lesbianism or intercourse of an erotic character between women, and yet there are several women whose friendship with other women does carry a taint and a suspicion, simply because these women are notoriously sapphic in their loves. On the other hand a great friendship may exist between two ordinary women and nobody would think of imputing to them improper motives.' It closes on his father: the man who deserted his wife, 'has since been divorced for a second time', wrote pamphlets and gave lectures advocating 'a sort of polygamy which is neither more nor less than free love. This is the man who has been made into a hero by the English people and the press, who is cheered in the streets by the mob, and who has crowned his career by dishonouring and driving out of England his son who now writes to you.' Signed Alfred Douglas HIS OWN REVISIONS, which are the most telling thing on the sheet: 'My opinion is that no such taint would attach to friendships between those of the same sex unless the ~~[taint?]~~ [inserted: suspicion] was justified by facts.' The struck word is read as 'taint' by Lovelle and queried; I had first read it as 'trust'. 'taint' is the likelier reading and the sense supports it - he had already used 'taint' earlier in the same sentence, caught the repetition, and replaced the second with 'suspicion' carried above the line. 'trust' would create no repetition to fix. He also strikes a false start before 'Thus', deletes 'then' after 'do you anticipate', and inserts '[inserted: in London]' above the line after 'there are several women' - localising the claim after writing it. The quotation marks round 'carry a taint & a suspicion' appear to be him quoting Stead's own phrasing back at him. NOT YET FULLY TRANSCRIBED: the passages quoted here were read off the inverted-and-mirrored positives, not collated line by line across all six sides. A full transcription belongs in TRANSCRIPTIONS.json if this letter is ever cited. READABLE COPIES: because the negatives are white-on-black and laterally reversed, and cannot be collated against a transcription as they stand, inverted-and-mirrored positives of all seven are kept alongside them at `3286-third-party-a-h/derived-positives/`, with a README there recording exactly what was done to each. Those are ours, not the archive's - inverted, flipped, cropped, contrast-stretched, gamma-lifted and unsharp-masked, and the unsharp mask thickens thin strokes. Read from the positives; verify against the negatives. No marks claim should rest on a processed image.

'Eighty' Club papers: a blank printed subscription banker's order, and a letter from J. M. B. Bruce, Secretary, 3 Middle Temple Lane, 5 July 1888, informing a member of his election to the Club. WILDE IS NAMED AS PROPOSER - 'You were proposed by O. Wilde and Seconded by W. S. Shurrington' - the recipient being A. Clifton Esq. The Eighty Club was a Liberal political club; the note explains that candidates must be prepared for election by the Club unless they shall have signified their willingness to take part in political work on behalf of the Liberal Party

Fabienne Hillyard to H. Montgomery Hyde, 17 May 1956, 28 Sloane Court East - sending him three letters from Wilde to AIMEE LOWTHER, 'please use them as you like'. She adds, in the margin, what she calls 'the unpublished poem to A. Lowther': 'Your eyes are deep green pools / In which the sun has gazed, / And passing left a golden ray.' - 'He called it Hazel Eyes'

TRANSCRIPTS in Fabienne Hillyard's hand, headed 'Letters from Oscar Wilde to Miss A. Lowther' - three letters from the Hotel d'Alsace, April-May 1898, on placing a poem called 'The Poet' in a Paris magazine over his own signature, on Gaston Rossi and Fontainebleau, and on what matters in writing: 'subject is no matter: style, treatment, vision, symbol, those are the important things'. One carries 'your friendship is a blossom on the crown of thorns that my life has borne'. NOT autographs - a later hand's copies, and no emphasis claim can rest on them

TRANSCRIPT of a further Wilde letter to Aimee Lowther, Royal Albion Hotel, Brighton, dated by the copyist [1892-3?] - 'I always want to kill people who bring me letters of introduction. Indeed everybody in the world should be either killed or kissed.' Again a copy, not an autograph

Fabienne Hillyard to H. Montgomery Hyde, 11 July 1955, 28 Sloane Court East - dating the Wilde-Lowther letters. 'I was trying to discover the exact date of Oscar Wilde's letters to Aimee, and in the search found another one I am enclosing. The one you have, marked 24, was written between 97 and 1900. The one I enclose comes immediately before the other one you have, and was written - I believe - in April or May 1898.' She dates the letter with an eye on posterity 'as a protest against people who put no more than Sunday or Tuesday on their letters'
Envelope from Mrs F. Hillyard to H. Montgomery Hyde MP at the House of Commons, 1957, and a postcard: 'Would you very kindly send me the O.W. letters, as a friend of mine is very anxious to see them'

Fabienne Hillyard to H. Montgomery Hyde, 29 November - she should long ago have acknowledged the three Wilde letters but was ill; and one is missing. 'You have forgotten to return to me the one from Royal Albion Hotel, Brighton, with Indeed everybody should either be killed or kissed. You may remember I found it in the book, but not stuck in, in the envelope, and sent you the letter (not the envelope).' She adds 'of course I'd give you the first refusal of the letters if I ever want - or need - to sell them'

H. Montgomery Hyde to Mrs F. Hillyard, 6 December 1957 - the other side of the missing letter. 'Are you quite certain that the letter from the Royal Albion Hotel which you mention was included amongst those which you sent me? I have no recollection of such a letter. I have already been through all my files and papers on Wilde and can find no trace. You say that you found it in a book, but I do not remember you having told me about this. I am rather worried about it, so please have a look round at your end and let me know'

Vyvyan Holland to Franklin P. Rolfe, 30 October 1940, The Judge's Lodgings, County Rooms, Leicester - consenting to publication of Wilde's letters, with a warning: 'I have no objection at all to your publishing the letters in question, but I think it just as well to warn you that Lord Alfred Douglas is still alive and that if the letters contain anything derogatory to him he is almost certain to institute libel proceedings. He always does!' The other side of the Douglas refusal at images 26-27, in the same month

Sir Travers Humphreys to H. Montgomery Hyde, October 1946 - on writing the preface to Hyde's edition of the Wilde trials for the Notable British Trials series. Humphreys had been junior counsel for Wilde in 1895. He comments on the plan for the book, on what he can contribute 'from my own view and from my own recollection', and on the sentence: 'I do not agree with you that the sentence was excessive'

William Hodge & Company (James H. Hodge, Director) to Mr Justice Humphreys, 2 and 8 October 1946, with his reply in copy - the commissioning correspondence for the Notable British Trials volume. Hodge writes that 'Mr H. Montgomery Hyde, Barrister-at-Law, has kindly agreed to act as Editor of this volume', that 'It seems to us that Wilde's trials should be properly recorded without prejudice', and asks Humphreys for a preface 'from one who was so closely associated with the trials'. Humphreys replies that he had thought the trials already published with the shorthand notes, has no objection to writing a preface, and notes that a recent Life of Wilde contained 'a number of egregious mistakes about the Trials'. Hodge answers that the only existing publication, 'Oscar Wilde Three Times Tried' (1912), is long out of print and scarce, and that the new text will be based 'from the current reports, the judge's notes and a transcription by a shorthand writer in the Courts at the time'

Sir Travers Humphreys to H. Montgomery Hyde, 13 January, 20 February and 2 March 1947, Royal Courts of Justice - returning the draft of Hyde's introduction with comments. He asks that passages be omitted, thinks three passages 'require amending as statements of law', and objects to a remark attributed to Willie Mathews 'which I do not believe he ever said'. He adds 'I have never read Hesketh Pearson's book so can only comment on what you say is the tenor of his remarks about E. Clarke', and 'I should like to see your Introduction in its final form as The Introduction is the Book'. In March he agrees a story may be used but notes 'I am no lover of twice-told anecdotes' and asks that it be put in the first person 'as it was to me he said it'. He ends: 'I have no photo of myself as a barrister'

Sir Travers Humphreys to H. Montgomery Hyde, May-June 1948, from Judges' Lodgings at Salisbury and Dorchester - on signing the fifty limited copies of the Notable British Trials Wilde volume while on circuit, with his itinerary; a dry note on the publishers, 'They are Scotch - and not extravagant in their ideas!'; and finally 'Herewith 54 signatures, accuracy not guaranteed since they follow upon 6 hours writing in Court. I shall want a copy for the Inner Temple Library and one for the Garrick Club'

Sir Travers Humphreys to H. Montgomery Hyde, 20 September 1948, 47 Castlebar Road, Ealing - the last of the sequence, and the sharpest. 'It is now nearly 3 months since the book on Oscar Wilde was published and so far I have not received one halfpenny from Hodge and Co for the trouble I took at your request in writing a foreword and signing my name 50 times solely for the purpose of enabling the publishers to charge more for the book and the autographed copies. You know more of the ways of publishers than I do. Will you be good enough to tell me whether this is the practice in the trade? If so I will be careful to have a written contract the next time I am invited to do anything of the sort. With newspapers I know it to be unnecessary as they pay and pay well without being asked'

items.title: Third-Party correspondence to or from Margaret Lumley Brown

matches.what: Margaret Lumley Brown to Robert Ross, 49 Edgware Road, Hyde Park, 25 January 1914. She writes to say she has been receiving communications by clairaudience and automatic writing from someone 'who in the end came continually and who said he was Oscar Wilde', and encloses her record of the conversations. She is anxious to be believed: 'I am sure you will believe that I have not written for any vulgar purpose or notoriety', and 'I have sent the writings in good faith'
Envelope, marked Private and registered, to Robert Ross Esq., Mayfair Chambers, Reform Club, Pall Mall

Ten typescript pages of the purported dialogues, set out as 'X.' and numbered replies. NOT BY WILDE, AND NOT EVIDENCE OF ANYTHING HE SAID OR WROTE. They are a medium's productions of 1914, fourteen years after his death, and they are dangerous precisely because they read plausibly: aphoristic, epigrammatic, and full of the right proper nouns - Bosie, Sebastian Melmoth, the Ballad, Catholicism, Tiberius and Caligula. Nothing from these pages may be quoted as Wilde, cited as a source, or entered on the relationship map as anything other than what it is. What the item does document is real and belongs to Ross's story, not Wilde's: that by 1914 people were writing to his literary executor claiming to have him on the line

A. B. Johnson to E. C. Stedman, 23 January 1882, Treasury Department, Office of the Light-House Board, Washington - a third-party letter that catches Wilde mid-tour. 'Oscar Wilde was brought to the Cosmos last night and I was not one of those who bowed down and worshipped him. But he has been feted here as the papers will tell you. I am glad to hear that you have been conspicuous by your absence from among those who are yet to regret their homaging of the alleged aesthete.' The first half is on Stedman's own poetry

Postcard photograph, 'Par les dieux jumeaux - Tous les monstres ne sont pas en Afrique!', addressed to Lieut. H. V. Jervis Read, 34 Cambridge Road, Battersea Park, postmarked Wimbledon 27 February 1915 - congratulations on recovery, and a note about Major Gerald Norcott of the North Lancashire Regiment at the War Office. Signed with initials
Letter in French, 'Cher Demoiselle', signed Sarah Bernhardt - on a volume sent to her and a journey to London. Correspondent identification to be confirmed

Envelope to Jane Elgee, 34 Leeson Street, Dublin, postmarked Paris 15 Mars 1866, with a red wax seal on the verso - addressed to Wilde's mother under her maiden name, four years before he was born... to be checked; Speranza had married in 1851, so the name and date want verifying

Sir Frederic Leighton to Mrs Oscar Wilde, 2 Holland Park Road, Kensington - presenting his compliments and regretting that a previous engagement for the 1st of July will prevent his coming; with a second leaf, 'from Whistler himself, for her amiable invitation for that day'

C. S. Millard ('Stuart Mason') to a correspondent, 28 July 1925, The Bungalow, 8 Abercorn Place - enclosing his pamphlet 'impugning the authenticity of the play called For Love of the King which was published a few years under Oscar Wilde's name'. 'I take full responsibility for issuing it and have not done so without considering the possible consequences nor without making sure of my facts... I venture to think that the correspondence discloses one of the most remarkable literary forgeries of recent years'

Printed pamphlet, 'Who Wrote For Love of the King?', C. S. Millard ('Stuart Mason'), 1925 - the full correspondence, twelve numbered items, between Millard, Methuen & Co, T. Werner Laurie, Walter Hutchinson and Mrs Wodehouse Pearse, June-July 1925, with Millard's letters to The Times and the Times Literary Supplement. He argues the play published under Wilde's name is a forgery, notes that Robert Ross refused to include it in the collected edition, that Vyvyan Holland and Wilde's literary executor were not consulted, and that Mrs Wodehouse Pearse 'offered to sell me six of these letters, all of which I have no hesitation in saying were forgeries'. He challenges her to produce the original manuscript in Wilde's handwriting. 'The evidence against her is overwhelming'

Publisher's advertisement leaf for Stuart Mason's Bibliography of Oscar Wilde, T. Werner Laurie, with an introductory note by Robert Ross - 630 pages, over a hundred reproductions, and 'the unpublished scenario of the lost play, The Cardinal of Avignon, and the suppressed dedication to The Ballad of Reading Gaol', with press opinions

Myers & Co (Booksellers) Ltd, 80 New Bond Street, to P. R. Henderson, 16 November 1948 - valuing a copy of Wilde's After Reading, After Berneval, 'being one of the five copies for presentation and being an association copy of some merit', at 25 pounds

H. Montgomery Hyde to Grant Richards, 11 June 1947, with Richards's reply - on the manuscript of a letter from LORD ALFRED DOUGLAS to W. T. STEAD, 'written immediately after the Oscar Wilde trial in 1895', which has come into Hyde's possession and which he can find no trace of in the files of the Review of Reviews. He proposes to print it, with Stead's editorial comments, as an appendix to his Notable British Trials volume. Richards, who was with Stead at the time, replies that he has 'no memory of its arrival nor of any conversation about it', though he thinks he would have remembered 'a long and poignant letter from Douglas to W. T. Stead'

Grant Richards to H. Montgomery Hyde, 22 October 1947, from 3 Avenue des Citronniers, Monte Carlo, with Hyde's reply of 21 October - Richards has been too ill to write, will lunch with Hyde when back in England, has 'of course seen Mrs Mimi Le Gallienne', and asks about 'the one matter in particular'. Hyde sends the script of his BBC appreciation of Richard Le Gallienne, broadcast 9 October 1947, and answers that 'the one matter in particular is no longer of any importance'

Arthur Ransome to Robert Ross, from Stockholm, 11 June [1913] - thanking him for a long and amusing letter 'which found me in a most affecting green and yellow and alligator cowardly depression'. He is going to Finland, care of Mrs Gallibrand, Terijoki, and asks Ross to telegraph if anything happens; 'I do not want to come home ever again, except those and other people who do not weigh. There is never a melodrama, but I never so absurd as my wife turning up. I shared exactly her own little private melodrama of my own'. Signed Arthur Ransome

Provenance note by C. A. Marchan, 21 January 1928, The Barn House, Streatham - 'This letter from Arthur Ransome to Robert Ross came to me except purchase I made from the executor of Christopher Stoker Millard (Stuart Mason) on 20th January 1928. Millard died on 22nd Nov 1927. The purchase was made at The Bungalow at 8 Abercorn Place N.W.8', with marginal notes identifying Ross as executor of Wilde's estate and Millard as Wilde's bibliographer

Lennox Robinson to H. Montgomery Hyde, 26 June 1954, 20 Longford Terrace, Monkstown, with Hyde's reply of 29 June - on the W. B. YEATS LETTER TO DOWDEN written during the Wilde trials, which Robinson had copied for him: 'It is all in his (Yeats's) handwriting, there are certain erasures which I did not think worth reproducing.' Hyde calls it 'an extremely interesting letter' which 'proves conclusively the points about the money and the yacht which have sometimes been doubted'. Robinson adds that a plaque is to go up in Westland Row

COPY of W. B. YEATS to Edward Dowden, 19 May [1895], 3 Blenheim Row, Bedford Park - written during the trials. 'I went to try and see Wilde today and to tell him how much I sympathised with him in his trouble. He has left Oakley Street but they told me there much about his movements. A yacht and a very large sum of money was placed at his disposal and all settled for his flight but he refused to go. He says he will stand it out and for the worst and no matter how it turns out work on. He will not go down, they said, or drink, or take poison.' Yeats had found some of the Dublin literary men sympathetic, and asks Dowden to write to Wilde, at 146 Oakley Street, Chelsea
Blank leaf with a pencil flourish - verso of the Yeats copy

Robert Ross to a correspondent, 15 July - on the collected edition of Wilde's works coming out in the autumn, the Greek and Polish translations, and the difficulty of making a complete uniform edition
Wrapper: 'Extract from letter of Robert Ross describing Wilde's death. Please return to Robert Ross, Hotel Drexelmore'

TYPESCRIPT, 'Letter from Robert Ross describing last days of Oscar Wilde', 14 December 1900, thirteen pages - the fullest contemporary account of Wilde's death, and the source behind every biography of it. Ross's telegram from Wilde, 'Terribly weak, please come'; Wilde's grievance against Frank Harris over the Daventry money, 'Frank has deprived me of my only source of income by taking a play on which I could have always raised 100 pounds'; the absinthe at a Latin Quarter cafe; his hair 'slightly tinged with grey' for the first time; Dr Tucker and Dr Kleiss; the dream 'that he had been supping with the dead', to which Reggie Turner replied 'My dear Oscar you were probably the life and soul of the party'. Then the end: Ross fetching FATHER CUTHBERT DUNNE of the Passionists, who 'administered baptism and extreme unction - Oscar could not take the eucharist'; 'you know I had always promised to bring a priest to Oscar when he was dying, and I felt rather guilty that I had so often dissuaded him from becoming a catholic'; the death rattle, 'I had never heard anything like it before, it sounded like the horrible turning of a crank and it never ceased until the end'; the passing at ten minutes to two. Then the practical horror: the assumed name Melmoth on the hotel register being 'contrary to French Law', the Mairie and the Commissaire de Police, 'Dying in Paris is really a very difficult and expensive luxury for a foreigner'; the District Doctor asking whether Oscar had committed suicide or was murdered; the rosary Ross had given him laid round his neck and a Franciscan medal on his breast; Maurice Gilbert's photograph, whose flashlight failed. And the funeral at St Germain des Pres and Bagneux, with the list of the fifty-six present and of the wreaths - Douglas, More Adey, Reginald Turner, Ricketts and Shannon, Mrs Leverson, Frank Harris, the Mercure de France - and Ross's own laurel wreath 'A tribute to his literary achievements and distinction', inside which he tied the names of all who had been kind to Wilde during or after his imprisonment. It closes on Reggie Turner, who 'had the worst time of all in many ways - he experienced all the horrible uncertainty, and the appalling responsibility of which he did not know the extent'

ROBERT ROSS TO FRANK HARRIS, 1 February 1917, 40 Half Moon Street, five pages - answering Harris's letters of October to January in sequence while Harris wrote his life of Wilde. On Shaw and George Moore; on Douglas objecting to 'the detached and patronising attitude' of Ross's preface to De Profundis; on the myth 'invented by Douglas himself and subsequently maintained by his family' that Wilde was no writer; and on his own function since 1900, 'to try and get the books and plays a fair hearing and a fair reading and to obtain some benefit from their sale for Wilde's children'. The money: when Douglas inherited 25,000 pounds from Queensberry in 1900, 'Wilde still being alive, I asked him to pay off Wilde's debts and thereby acquire copyrights, which I offered to administrate on his behalf until he was repaid. Instead, he bought a stud at Chantilly and got through the money in less than six months.' And 'Douglas never forgave either himself or me for having rejected such a very good business proposal.' Family news: Vyvyan Holland 'married and is still alive and is in the Field Artillery, and at the front'; 'Cyril, the elder boy, was killed at Neuve Chapelle on May 9th, 1915'. On the authorship of 'The Priest and the Acolyte' - 'It was written by an undergraduate called Bloxam. He is now dead.' A postscript on a letter Cyril Holland wrote before leaving India

Cyril Holland to a correspondent, 1 July 1914, Club of Western India, Poona - written on hearing of the Ross v. Crossland case, four weeks before the war and a year before he was killed. He asks that his father's estate defray all trial expenses, 'if estate will not run to this, that I wish to pay expenses out of personal income'; that the estate be at Ross's personal disposal, 'capital, copyright, interest, everything, to do with what he should think best to prevent the recurrence of any such future annoyance by Lord A.D.'; and 'You will inform Mr Ross that this is no Quixotic offer. It is profoundly serious. I regard the quarrel as mine as much as his. My honour is more to me than money'

MEMORANDUM prepared by Robert Ross's solicitors as Administrator of Wilde's estate, for valuation of the literary and dramatic estate - the financial history in five pages. Wilde 'died on November 30th, 1900, an undischarged bankrupt'; the copyrights had passed to the Official Receiver; Sir George Alexander applied to purchase the rights in Lady Windermere's Fan and The Importance of Being Earnest, and Hargrove & Co's offer of 100 pounds for each was accepted 'in spite of the protests of Mr Robert Ross'. The revival of the plays and the publication of De Profundis 'caused a renewal of interest in Mr Wilde's works generally which enabled the Official Receiver in Bankruptcy to pay all the creditors 20 shillings in the pound with 4 per cent interest. The bankruptcy was accordingly annulled on February 2nd, 1906.' Letters of Administration were granted to Ross in August 1906, 'the estate being valued at 100 pounds'. It lists the copyrights transferred, and those Ross presented to the estate out of his own property. It ends with Cyril Holland's death in action on 9 May 1915 and the descent of the estate

Rupert Hart-Davis to Dr Lawrence Clark Powell, Clark Library, 12 July 1954 - the letter that began the Complete Letters. 'I have just signed an agreement to publish a large volume called The Collected Letters of Oscar Wilde. Wilde's son, Vyvyan Holland, who owns all the copyrights, is a party to the agreement and has undertaken to give me all the help he can. The editor is to be Allan Wade.' He asks for photostats: 'We want, wherever possible, to take our texts from original letters or photostats, since so many garbled versions of Wilde's letters have appeared in many places through the years. I imagine that you must have the best collection of Wilde letters in the world'

PHOTOGRAPHIC NEGATIVE of a card from BERNARD SHAW, Ayot Saint Lawrence, 2 February 1949, white-on-black - on Wilde's talk. 'I took thankfully any part in the conversation. Wilde came to work... Wilde's testimony to the fact that Dorian Gray was a masterpiece of literature and morality.' Needs inverting and reading properly

Robert H. Sherard to Dr Norman, 1 and 3 March, 30 Culmington Road, Ealing - drafting his reply to Shaw's preface to Harris's book. Sherard's argument is that Wilde was not criminally responsible but 'the unfortunate victim of a terrible mental affliction', and he asks Norman, a medical man, whether he may cite him as an authority. The reasoning he sets out is period pseudo-science of the crudest kind and is recorded here as evidence of how Wilde's defenders argued in the 1930s, not as anything else. He also asks whether the recriminations against Douglas in the unpublished part of De Profundis prove 'that under certain circumstances the female awoke in his brain'

COPY of Hirosi Hirai, Kokusai Bunka Sinkokai, Marunouti, Tokyo, to Robert H. Sherard, 4 February 1939 - a Japanese scholar preparing 'the most complete and accurate and the largest biography that Japan has ever had', more than 600 pages, to be dedicated to Sherard 'who are so kind and generous in helping me and a sole authentic biographer of late Mr. Oscar Wilde'. He reports that Lord Alfred Douglas has sent him his own book inscribed 'A SNOOP-COPY PRESENTED FROM THE AUTHOR', that Douglas 'says he has no intention to explain or to make an excuse for it', and that the complete De Profundis 'shall not be published till 1960. I believe that it is an immense loss not merely of Mr. Wilde but also of English literature. Since French and German translations are published, I think, there is no meaning to suppress the English text only.' He asks Sherard for photostats and autographs

Sacheverell Sitwell to H. Montgomery Hyde, 25 July 1948, Weston Hall, Towcester - he has seen Cecil Beaton, who had just seen Vyvyan Holland and his wife in Australia. 'Vyvyan H. spoke of the horror of his early memories, which one can well believe; but, and this will interest you, apparently his wife had lately interviewed Wilde's old butler and coachman, who are both still living in the country. The latter drove Wilde and Alfred D. to the Old Bailey, and on their way Oscar W. stopped the carriage in St James's Street and went into a shop to buy a greyer tie. What can he have been thinking of? Both coachman and butler were very fond of him. Cecil Beaton took a note of the conversation in his diary'

Sacheverell Sitwell to H. Montgomery Hyde, 17 December 1955, Weston Hall - on RALPH HODGSON, the Georgian poet, who lived in Japan and is now 'somewhere right in the remote Middle West of America... apparently terribly poor'. Among his possessions 'is the account or report he wrote of Wilde's trial, which he attended as a journalist when he was about 25 years old. And, apparently, it is his account of it, in his writing, and with drawings of all the characters concerned. He is now 85.' Sitwell urges Hyde to get a record of it

H. Montgomery Hyde to Sacheverell Sitwell, 15 and 27 July 1948 - on ALFRED TAYLOR, and a defence of him that is worth having. 'I always understood that after his release he went to America. Your piquant story of his encounter with Alfred Douglas there confirms this impression.' And: 'Taylor seems to have been a wretched perverted character who was spoiled in his youth partly as a result of being left a considerable fortune by his father, who was, I believe, a wealthy cocoa manufacturer. It evidently amused Wilde to go to parties in his rooms but there is no evidence that Taylor did anything more than introduce or procure various youths, some of whom subsequently cut sorry figures in the witness box. Far from not blackmailing Wilde, Taylor might have saved his own skin by turning King's evidence, which he refused to do, and that at least should be remembered in his favour.' He also chases the Wilde-Douglas letters and the old butler and coachman
George Smalley to E. C. Stedman, 22 December 1881 - a note of introduction, 'I know the Oscar Wilde who brings you this'

To Mr Clements, New York, 6 January 1882 - a long letter on the American lecture circuit and on Wilde's arrival, complaining of London writers who take advantage of American hospitality: 'I do not blame a clever humbug like Wilde, for taking advantage of them each way and making all the money he can. He is a shrewd man of the world, and D'Oyly Carte is running him as a speculation.' The writer resents 'the influence of his titled patronesses' and predicts 'I do not think that Boston will not aid New York in making America again the rightful lampooning-stools of England. I suppose Wilde and Carte will cart away 100,000 dollars'
Dr Richard Strauss, in German, 4 October [19]-, from Garmisch - a short note, with a pencil annotation '(dealt with Wilde's Salome)'

To LADY WILDE, Tuesday 2 February 1891, 8 Richmond Terrace, Whitehall - a friend writing about her patriotic feeling and about the Irish question, and about his wife's writing. 'I write to ask you to tell Sir William that the smoky times are also that his kindest regard for you'. Signature not yet read; the second leaf runs on about ambrosia and 'his bachelor abode'

REGINALD TURNER to Vyvyan Holland, 20 December 1933, 15 Viale Milton, Florence - Turner had been at Wilde's deathbed thirty-three years before, and is writing to Wilde's younger son. He apologises for the delay, having been ill: 'I have been back from Switzerland a fortnight and all the time ill and now I am going on Monday to Milan with my doctor to see a specialist.' He hopes to have Vyvyan and Thelma in his own newly renovated apartment. Signed 'R.T.'

REGINALD TURNER to Vyvyan Holland, 29 August 1938, Hotel Meurice, Ouchy, Lausanne - four sides, and the fullest of the Turner letters here. 'Having seen your name and address in the New Statesman I feel constrained to write to you.' He is 76, an exile of long standing, and writes about Italy under Mussolini and about England on the eve of war: 'I am now old. If I were living I arrived at l'age qui n'a pas dire vous nommer - viz. 67 - but as it is the same of thank it our Prime Minister - whom the last has and patience - I take courage.' He is scathing about Fascist Italy and the radio - 'you can't understand the reason people have for moaning about when they hear the Radio (for sound) and the Cinema for sight; one can see all the horrors for a small sum in a fairly comfortable seat'. He asks Vyvyan to write again, and mentions reading Virginia Woolf and re-reading Henry James

Envelopes to Vyvyan Holland Esq., 41 Carlyle Square, Chelsea, London S.W.3 - postmarked Lausanne-Ouchy, Chelsea 30 August 1938, and Firenze 21 October 1939, the last endorsed in pencil 'Reggie Turner's last letter to me'

To a correspondent, 3 August, 199 Strand [Dublin?] - 'I have an uneasy feeling that something went wrong with my reply to your kind letter sending me the Oscar Wilde cartoon. I presume that you have no objection to my using it with suitable acknowledgment. I enclose what may be of interest to you - a photo of Oscar's brother known as Henry Wilson than Sir William fathered about 1838 and who died a year after him; also an up to date photo of the Wildes' house.' Signed Terence de Vere White. The reference is to Wilde's illegitimate half-brother

Photographer's envelope, The Green Studio Ltd, 118 St Stephen's Green West, Dublin, inscribed 'Dr Henry Wilson, illegitimate brother of Oscar Wilde' - the wrapper for the photograph mentioned in the Terence de Vere White letter at images 83-84. The photograph itself is not present

Tradesman's bill, A la Toison d'Or, Naudin, Chemisier, 1 Boulevard des Capucines, Paris, 26 September 1899, made out to 'Monsieur Melmoth, Hotel d'Alsace, rue des Beaux Arts' - a shirt, receipted with a revenue stamp. Wilde buying a shirt under the exile name, fourteen months before he died; the verso carries the shopkeeper's pencil arithmetic

CONSTANCE WILDE to Arthur Clifton, 23 December 1889, 16 Tite Street - 'If you are in town and not engaged on Xmas Day, it will give us great pleasure if you will join us at dinner at 8 o'c. Please telegraph early tomorrow morning if you can come or not.' Docketed on the verso in Wilde's initials, 'O.W.'

CONSTANCE WILDE to Alice, 26 February 1892, 16 Tite Street - a letter of condolence on a death. 'My heart is bleeding for you in your great trouble and I don't know how to give you one word of comfort. All comfort seems so cold when one is in very great grief; only the Divine Comforter can help, and I do hope and pray that He may enter into your heart and take up His abode there, and fill you with the joy of His presence. The dear mother must be so happy now, having passed safely through all the storms of life, and safe in harbour at last. Oscar is not at home at present, but I know that he will join with me in expressions of sympathy with you and Henriette'

CONSTANCE WILDE to Mr Corney Grain, 16 Tite Street - on a girl who wants to go on the stage. 'I have conveyed your reply to my friend, but I cannot tell whether she will end by calling on you or not. People always seem to me to think that there is a fortune to be made on the stage, and so many girls write to me for opinions on the subject! This Miss Faulkner I have known for many years, and as she had seen you at my grandfather's house, she applied to me for an introduction. She is very nice, rather pretty, and bright, so she might get on, if she could get an opening'

Prof. Rolfe(?) of the Clark Library circle to Vyvyan Beresford Holland, 1 October 1940, 51 Doraleage Road, Newton Highlands, Massachusetts - on typed Clark Library letterhead. He seeks permission, as owner of the copyright, to publish the Clark Library's Wilde letters, 'chiefly from Reading, to More Adey and Robert Ross'. He describes declining A. J. A. Symons's proposal that they collaborate on a two-volume edition, 'because I doubted that a collaboration between two men personally unknown to each other and six thousand miles apart would prove satisfactory to either'. He disclaims any profit: 'I have absolutely no interest in profiting financially from the publication of the letters. I desire merely to edit them with a simple introduction calling attention to their great importance.' The other side of the Douglas and Vyvyan Holland exchanges of the same month in item 3286

items.title: Third-Party correspondence to or from W. F. Morse

matches.what: Not correspondence. Nine printed lecture-booking verification forms, 'Mr Oscar Wilde's Lectures, Season 1883-84' and 'Season 1884-5', issued by W. F. Morse as manager of Wilde's lectures in America and England from 40 Norfolk Street, Strand, and filled in by local secretaries with city, date, society, subject, terms, hall, hour and hotel. Several are countersigned G. W. Appleton. No letter to or from Wilde is present, and nothing here bears on the relationship map. They are, however, a precise itinerary source: Warminster, Colchester, Leicester, Newport, Wolverhampton, Birmingham, Northampton, Haywards Heath and the Royal Aquarium at Great Yarmouth, with the lecture titles ('The House Beautiful', 'Personal Impressions of America', 'The Value of Art in Modern Life', 'Dress') and the fees
